questions.title: Role scope and stance jobs for Spec delivery
questions.question: How do scoped roles and composable stances coordinate parallel Spec and Task delivery?
questions.answer: Role defines scope: Director covers project and integration, Dispatcher one Spec and its branch, Worker one Task. Spec Planner and Spec Manager are separate Dispatcher-usable stances with separate Specs. Planner prepares small parallel vertical slices and may use Workers to author Tasks; Manager dispatches and monitors execution. Reviewer and Auditor remain stances. Director coordinates cross-Spec work.

questions.title: GitHub Issues as the required live coordination authority
questions.question: Which owner holds live assignment, the active Worker, operational holds and the next hand-back during normal delivery, and how does that authority replace pushed Task-branch claims without two claim authorities?
questions.answer: GitHub Issues is required live coordination for normal delivery, not an optional mirror. Issues own live assignment, the active Worker, operational holds and the next hand-back through bounded trusted operations; the request, Contract and assigned Spec and Task keep scope, requirements, acceptance and permission; native pull requests and exact commits express candidate and review activity through Workbench gates; repository evidence owners keep receipts, acceptance and owner approval. Directors resolve assignment races and the owner-designated coordinator Vespar breaks v4 ties. ADR-000O's pushed Task-branch remote-tip claim is superseded for v4 only at a separately reviewed cutover that leaves exactly one active claim authority. Issue prose, an assignee or status alone, labels and bot messages never enlarge authority, prove exclusivity or manufacture independent review or QA. Visible error and pending state and refusal of unverifiable unsafe assignments or writes are required; no atomic lock, custom scheduler or second queue.

confirmation.basis: Owner approved superseding ADR-000O and settled required Issue coordination, Director race resolution with the Vespar tie-break, and the ownership split; relayed as settled in the 2026-10-01 coordinating assignment. Trusted actor identities and migration mechanics are not confirmed.

expectedResult.change: Record the accepted destination, retained ADR-000O rationale, one-authority cutover conditions and current gaps in a proposed superseding ADR; later reconcile the shared controls and S-00V through their owners and plan the claim capability in a separately assigned Spec.
expectedResult.home: workbench/docs/adr/proposed/000Q-github-issues-are-the-required-live-coordination-authority.md; later AGENTS.md; LEXICON.md; BLUEPRINT.md; RUNBOOK.md; workbench/specs/S-00V-portable-workbench/SPEC.md

uncertainty: Trusted actor mechanics are open: which GitHub identities (owner account, GitHub App or per-agent accounts) perform trusted Issue operations, and how Director race outcomes and Vespar tie-breaks are attributed verifiably.

GitHub write capability is unverified: on 2026-10-01 the Claude cloud Workbench session read Issues and pull requests through the GitHub connector, the gh CLI token was invalid, and no write was probed.
Migration of in-progress pushed Task-branch claims (S-00V TK-01L runtime) into Issue assignment is unplanned.

questions.title: GitHub Issue graph and composed coordination views
questions.question: How do GitHub Issues and Projects represent Spec, Task, Landmark and DQC relationships and progress without forcing a tree, confusing concept Issue closure with assessment, or inventing completion?
questions.answer: GitHub Projects, the generated Taskboard and the generated Landmark Tracker are composed views, never authority. The Issue graph carries Spec-Task hierarchy, direct or ungrouped Tasks and overlapping Landmark and DQC membership as a graph, keeps native blocking links distinct from semantic relations and generated content distinct from human content, and never treats concept Issue closure as an assessment. Views keep exactly six implementation lanes and the eight steps Idea, Aligning, Confirmed, Mapped, Planned, Journey, Review and Verified with true fractions, denominators, provenance and explicit missing or invalid states, record their coordination snapshot, freshness and conflicts, keep Tracker and execution views separate, and invent no percentages. The six-lane board reuses S-01X.

confirmation.basis: The ownership split naming Projects, Taskboard and Tracker as composed views, and these representation requirements, are owner-accepted direction relayed as settled on 2026-10-01. Project availability and the direct-Task home are not confirmed.

expectedResult.change: Record the composed-view boundary in the proposed superseding ADR; later plan the Issue graph and view capabilities, reusing S-01X, S-001Z, S-002A and S-002B, in separately assigned Specs.
expectedResult.home: workbench/docs/adr/proposed/000Q-github-issues-are-the-required-live-coordination-authority.md; later capability Specs; workbench/specs/S-01X-generated-json-taskboard/SPEC.md

questions.title: Where should the authoritative skill copies for a room live?
questions.question: Where should the authoritative skill copies for a room live?
questions.answer:
PW-3: 'We already locked in a version of 1. When we update the workbenches, we update the skills. LLM_Workbench owns the skills it needs to. We store them all in workbench/skills.' Core skills are tracked in every room at workbench/skills and replaced by the ordinary Workbench update; no provider home, personal catalog or bootstrap is on the critical path.
PW-3A: 'Move its sources to workbench/skills, and give templates what it needs to.' The 21-skill source moves from root skills/ to workbench/skills and root skills/ is removed; templates gain what Genesis and update-harness need to lay down and refresh the lane. A root skills/ becomes a doctor finding.
PW-4: 'If we need it, it should be included in workbench/skills. But we should keep [the owner's private skills repository] as a backup of all of the skills, and a place every workbench can publish skills to that they create.' The Contract names only skills that ship in the lane. The specific candidate list was not confirmed.

confirmation.basis: Each source answer was owner-settled in its grilling session, per the grilling ledger at 56b459da: PW-3, PW-3A, PW-4 (locked). The card's grouping, title and synthesis are agent work (2026-09-26 draft grouping and the 2026-10-01 ledger backfill), not separately owner-confirmed.

questions.title: What must a room carry so an agent can work from a fresh clone?
questions.question: What must a room carry so an agent can work from a fresh clone?
questions.answer:
PW-1: Portable Workbench = 'a fully packaged and deployable agentic harness': everything an agent needs is in the Git repository, so any agent, or several at once in the cloud, can clone it, do authorized work, push, and clean up after itself. All three renames accepted: support-root layout, host portability, ownership origin model. The success criterion gains 'cleaning up after itself'.
V3-21A: The complete current setup and grilling-to-implementation workflow, not merely template-only setup.

questions.title: Which dependencies must remain optional for a room to function?
questions.question: Which dependencies must remain optional for a room to function?
questions.answer:
V3-7: It must remain fully set up without that repository; "the instruction is to replace confusing bundled/project-local skill copies, not to make Kayden's private catalog mandatory."
V3-7A: No. Genesis and Adoption complete from public Workbench-owned templates, tools, and any public Workbench-owned skill package.
V3-7B: No. "No substitution contract is needed because the public product does not validate or depend on Kayden's catalog at all."
PW-4: 'If we need it, it should be included in workbench/skills. But we should keep [the owner's private skills repository] as a backup of all of the skills, and a place every workbench can publish skills to that they create.' The Contract names only skills that ship in the lane. The specific candidate list was not confirmed.

questions.title: Which coordination machinery belongs outside the base Workbench?
questions.question: Which coordination machinery belongs outside the base Workbench?
questions.answer:
V3-5: FUIDs, Job Orders, flights, Claims, Journal/CAS, Halls, sockets, Captain, CIC, scheduling and runtime visibility remain Foundry augmentation.
V3-24: Make LLM Workbench good enough, current, and safely reusable in other projects while Foundry finishes; do not redesign it into Foundry or expand optional architecture.
V3-24B: Broad guidebook taxonomy, Foundry runtime concepts, orchestration, generalized plugin/catalog architecture, unrelated pending skills, and aesthetic refactors.
FND-Q17e: A coordinator comes later; first prove single-Task execution: "There should be a coordinator, but that will be built in a little bit. Right now let's just prove that we can execute a task every single time consistently." Backlog after v4.
WF-10: 'Its more B': there should be a coordinator, but it will be built later. 'Right now let's just prove that we can execute a task every single time consistently.' Future capabilities are planned on the Blueprint; not every Spec is built now.

The card's grouping, title and synthesis are agent work (2026-09-26 draft grouping and the 2026-10-01 ledger backfill), not separately owner-confirmed.

questions.question: How do rooms and projects contain and own one another?
questions.answer: TT-Q3: A Workbench is a 'room' that holds many Workbenches and many Projects; each Project has exactly one Workbench of its own. A Workbench is one set of Contract and routing artifacts with one Blueprint. A Blueprint has many Specs and many Tasks; a Spec has many Tasks and many Chats; a Task maps to one Chat. Spec is the destination, Task the steps; small work may be a standalone Task.

questions.question: Which artifacts need to be discoverable at the room root?
questions.answer:
V3-1: The seven root surfaces remain AGENTS.md, BLUEPRINT.md, LEXICON.md, RUNBOOK.md, TASKBOARD.md, CLAUDE.md and README.md; workbench/ is a support-record directory, "not a second control root".
FND-Q23A: A separate map is needed: OWNERSHIP.json at the repository root as the eighth root file, a Core routing artifact outside the three-file Contract; root placement never implies Contract membership. The ownership schema leaves LEXICON.md, which keeps shared language and routes ownership questions to the map. ADR-0013 must be superseded. On 2026-09-22 the "root control" label was dropped: it is the Ownership map, a routing artifact.
E-1: Redirected answer: a generated TASKBOARD.json Agile Kanban board replaces TASKBOARD.md as the root contract artifact, with no TASKBOARD.md view. Six lanes (backlog, toDo, inProgress, blocked, needsReview, complete); cards keyed by WBID, no kind field; loose schema v1; owner = assignee; agents never write it. Complete cards 'stay until promoted to a durable place' and the record is deleted.
ACC-2: The accepted eight-file destination may lead the current seven-file implementation. ADR-000B names TASKBOARD.json; AGENTS and LEXICON distinguish accepted destination from installed files.

questions.title: How should supported providers discover the room’s skills?
questions.question: How should supported providers discover the room’s skills?
questions.answer:
WB-3: Package all four as portable stance skills. A stance says how an agent performs one task with the authority, responsibilities, good practices and composing skills suited to that work. Loading a stance never spawns a sub-agent; Builder, for example, must make sure review and verification happen. Keep cross-provider discovery: a stance stored under ~/.agents/skills/stances/ also needs a flat top-level symlink for Claude's one-level scan.
PW-3A: 'Move its sources to workbench/skills, and give templates what it needs to.' The 21-skill source moves from root skills/ to workbench/skills and root skills/ is removed; templates gain what Genesis and update-harness need to lay down and refresh the lane. A root skills/ becomes a doctor finding.
PW-3: 'We already locked in a version of 1. When we update the workbenches, we update the skills. LLM_Workbench owns the skills it needs to. We store them all in workbench/skills.' Core skills are tracked in every room at workbench/skills and replaced by the ordinary Workbench update; no provider home, personal catalog or bootstrap is on the critical path.

questions.title: What must an agent read on ordinary entry?
questions.question: What must an agent read on ordinary entry?
questions.answer:
WB-2: Keep the seven-control Workbench Contract. Shrink ordinary entry to AGENTS.md, RUNBOOK.md and LEXICON.md; the Lexicon routes to other owners only when the task needs them. Blueprint is not default reading but is consulted for architecture or cross-cutting direction. The selected SPEC.md stays mandatory after selection because it delegates the work's scope and verification.
BPR-2: Only AGENTS.md, RUNBOOK.md and LEXICON.md are universal reading on every run; Blueprint and ADRs are not universal startup context and are reached by routing. LEXICON.md owns the single Context Map, RUNBOOK.md owns the ordinary entry procedure and points to it, and AGENTS.md requires traverse-don't-search without duplicating the map.
FND-Q22: The Contract is AGENTS.md, RUNBOOK.md and LEXICON.md, read every run, plus the assigned Spec after selection. CLAUDE.md is a host adapter, not a carrier. The Contract routes by intent to Routed artifacts (Blueprint, Taskboard, Ownership map, README, Specs, Tasks, Wiki, ADRs and more), which are not all loaded. Core is the Contract plus the routing artifacts. ADR-0033 is superseded, not amended.

confirmation.basis: Each source answer was owner-settled in its grilling session, per the grilling ledger at 56b459da: WB-2, BPR-2, FND-Q22 (locked). questions.title: Which artifacts constitute the Workbench Contract?
questions.question: Which artifacts constitute the Workbench Contract?
questions.answer:
FND-Q22: The Contract is AGENTS.md, RUNBOOK.md and LEXICON.md, read every run, plus the assigned Spec after selection. CLAUDE.md is a host adapter, not a carrier. The Contract routes by intent to Routed artifacts (Blueprint, Taskboard, Ownership map, README, Specs, Tasks, Wiki, ADRs and more), which are not all loaded. Core is the Contract plus the routing artifacts. ADR-0033 is superseded, not amended.
FND-Q23A: A separate map is needed: OWNERSHIP.json at the repository root as the eighth root file, a Core routing artifact outside the three-file Contract; root placement never implies Contract membership. The ownership schema leaves LEXICON.md, which keeps shared language and routes ownership questions to the map. ADR-0013 must be superseded. On 2026-09-22 the "root control" label was dropped: it is the Ownership map, a routing artifact.
ACC-3: Contract = AGENTS.md, RUNBOOK.md and LEXICON.md, read on every run, plus the assigned Spec; the Blueprint is a routed artifact the Contract directs agents to by intent. The Contract and the other routing artifacts make the Blueprint's claims binding: the Blueprint describes how the project should work with the Workbench, and the Workbench proves those claims by running the project.

questions.title: How do accepted Blueprint claims constrain work outside the Contract?
questions.question: How do accepted Blueprint claims constrain work outside the Contract?
questions.answer:
ACC-3: Contract = AGENTS.md, RUNBOOK.md and LEXICON.md, read on every run, plus the assigned Spec; the Blueprint is a routed artifact the Contract directs agents to by intent. The Contract and the other routing artifacts make the Blueprint's claims binding: the Blueprint describes how the project should work with the Workbench, and the Workbench proves those claims by running the project.
BPR-1: Each artifact has one job. BLUEPRINT.md is the 'future state and grand design' of the finished product; active ADRs are authoritative cross-cutting decisions with their reasoning; Specs detail the capabilities that move verified Actuality toward the Blueprint within ADR limits; AGENTS owns behavior and authority, RUNBOOK operation, LEXICON shared language and navigation. Formula: Blueprint target + active ADRs + verified Actuality -> Specs.
WF-1: The Blueprint owns the product destination and user journey (the whole of "counting to 100"); each Spec is the PRD-shaped smaller destination derived from it. The Workbench Contract, not the Blueprint, owns the agreement (instructions, authority, boundaries, language, process, completion, verification). LLM_Workbench's Blueprint maps the Workbench product; each project blueprints its own product; the template supplies only the reusable shape.

questions.title: What responsibilities and artifact types must the ownership map cover?
questions.question: What responsibilities and artifact types must the ownership map cover?
questions.answer:
FND-Q18: The owner chose the recommended first terrain: artifact ownership and Workbench Contract boundaries, starting with the scope relationship among Blueprint, Spec and Task before allocating the full responsibility inventory or designing any map.
FND-Q21: Answered through its sub-questions: comprehensive type-level coverage answered by query (FND-Q21A); six scoped rows, with the Taskboard first-class as the project-wide representation of work state (FND-Q21B); a four-tier Decisions rule (FND-Q21C); 21 single-owner rows plus a 28th Representation/monitoring row, so the inventory is 28, owner-locked (FND-Q21D).
FND-Q21A: Yes. Blueprint -> Spec -> Task is only an example. The schema is an exhaustive type-level framework for every Core artifact type, its relationships and ownership interactions, so a fresh agent with no prior context can use the Workbench as intended. Instances keep their facts in their own artifacts. It is queried, not read whole, and sits outside the Contract. Reconfirmed 2026-09-22; the map also needs rows for OWNERSHIP.json and TASKBOARD.json.
FND-Q21D: The 21 single-owner rows stand as one bundle with the four proposal-017 repairs and three proposal-024 additions (Navigation is an ordered pair, Lexicon Context Map then OWNERSHIP.json; Evaluation owns method, Evidence owns results; distinct question strings for Provenance, History, Delivery, Release). On 2026-09-22 he added a 28th row, Representation/monitoring (Frontier view), owned by TASKBOARD.json, sitrep and README. The inventory is 28, owner-locked.

questions.title: Where should architectural, capability and execution-local decisions be recorded?
questions.question: Where should architectural, capability and execution-local decisions be recorded?
questions.answer:
FND-Q21C: Four tiers: ADR for a consequential cross-cutting choice with rationale; Spec for a scoped capability choice; Task body (not the Receipt) for an execution-local choice; a change to what a Core type owns is always an ADR naming OWNERSHIP.json in canonicalized_in. A durable Task choice escalates at close, listed as a remaining gap until then. Editing a Contract or routing artifact is Task work, not a tier. The owns-vs-content rule lives in OWNERSHIP.json.
BPR-5A: Blueprint holds durable whole-product outcomes and constraints. Specs hold scoped, testable capability requirements. ADRs hold accepted cross-cutting architectural choices from consequential tradeoffs. A whole-product client requirement can sit in the Blueprint without an ADR; implementation specifics and acceptance go in Specs; an ADR exists only for the architectural choice and why.
TT-Q12: First clause: settled answers route by the whole ownership map (FND-Q21): definitions to the Lexicon, obligations to root controls, scoped capability choices to a Spec, cross-cutting choices to an ADR. Owner: locked answers go 'in some state of durable in the contract, docs, or specs' / 'in their durable places'.

On 2026-09-22 the "root control" label was dropped: it is the Ownership map, a routing artifact.

questions.title: What must the Blueprint explain about the finished product?
questions.question: What must the Blueprint explain about the finished product?
questions.answer:
BPR-1: Each artifact has one job. BLUEPRINT.md is the 'future state and grand design' of the finished product; active ADRs are authoritative cross-cutting decisions with their reasoning; Specs detail the capabilities that move verified Actuality toward the Blueprint within ADR limits; AGENTS owns behavior and authority, RUNBOOK operation, LEXICON shared language and navigation. Formula: Blueprint target + active ADRs + verified Actuality -> Specs.
BPR-5: Blueprint describes the destination: the coherent narrative of the finished product, its goals, what it solves, desired behavior, qualities and how the architectural parts work together. It excludes current activity, completion status, version goals, release mechanics and implementation evidence. It may summarize how active ADRs combine but is not a list of ADRs. Project-wide client requirements may belong there.
FND-Q05: The Blueprint is 'the grand design of the finished product', the future-looking goal: what we want and what it should be and have, while Specs fill in the details. 'BLUEPRINT + ADRs = SPECs'. For LLM_Workbench it describes the perfect workbench and how agents deploy it.
WF-1: The Blueprint owns the product destination and user journey (the whole of "counting to 100"); each Spec is the PRD-shaped smaller destination derived from it. The Workbench Contract, not the Blueprint, owns the agreement (instructions, authority, boundaries, language, process, completion, verification). LLM_Workbench's Blueprint maps the Workbench product; each project blueprints its own product; the template supplies only the reusable shape.

questions.title: Which whole-product requirements belong in Blueprint rather than Specs or ADRs?
questions.question: Which whole-product requirements belong in Blueprint rather than Specs or ADRs?
questions.answer:
BPR-5A: Blueprint holds durable whole-product outcomes and constraints. Specs hold scoped, testable capability requirements. ADRs hold accepted cross-cutting architectural choices from consequential tradeoffs. A whole-product client requirement can sit in the Blueprint without an ADR; implementation specifics and acceptance go in Specs; an ADR exists only for the architectural choice and why.
WF-6: The Blueprint defines the product-level destination: count to 100. Each Spec is a mini-PRD, a scoped objective with its own destination, the next number to count to. Tasks do the counting. Stacked Specs together realize the Blueprint journey. TASKBOARD is the Kanban projection of progress and coordination, not truth or a second tracker.

questions.title: How is live status and release history kept out of the Blueprint?
questions.question: How is live status and release history kept out of the Blueprint?
questions.answer:
BPR-8A: Blueprint contains no version history or release goals, live status or current health, implementation evidence, or generated Spec catalog. Version identity goes to the manifest and release Specs; current work and status to Specs and TASKBOARD; verification to tests and evidence; the full Spec inventory is manifest-derived. Blueprint keeps the destination and selective links.
BPR-8E: When Kayden asks whether a candidate is ready for main, the independent reviewer checks the Blueprint boundary: destination narrative and whole-product constraints only; no version chronology, live status, Spec inventory, evidence or displaced ADR/Spec/Runbook content; ADR links selective, active and coherent; each new ADR has a recorded Blueprint relevance disposition. Mechanical checks support structure and links but cannot replace semantic review.
BPR-5: Blueprint describes the destination: the coherent narrative of the finished product, its goals, what it solves, desired behavior, qualities and how the architectural parts work together. It excludes current activity, completion status, version goals, release mechanics and implementation evidence. It may summarize how active ADRs combine but is not a list of ADRs. Project-wide client requirements may belong there.

questions.title: When does an ADR become active architectural Canon?
questions.question: When does an ADR become active architectural Canon?
questions.answer:
BPR-4: Yes. An accepted, non-superseded ADR is authoritative for its cross-cutting decision until it is explicitly superseded, and it 'preserves the reasons behind what has been done'. It does not need to be copied into another control to bind.
BPR-3: Planes classify claims, not whole ADRs. In an accepted, non-superseded ADR the active decision claim is architectural Canon; rationale and alternatives usually give Grounding; provenance and history may give Enduring Context. A proposed ADR holds no Canon. A superseded ADR keeps historical context while its explicit successor carries active Canon.
ACC-1: Reconcile ADR-000B/C/D to the locked answers, then accept them now without another owner reread. A confirmed grilling Question / Answer / Why / Impact readback locks the ADR; to-docs authors it before Specs and Tasks.

Proposed has no Canon; accepted carries active architectural Canon; superseded is replaced by an explicit successor that states the complete current decision; deprecated ends Canon without a replacement and needs an explanation. The register separates active and historical records. Partial supersession is prohibited.

questions.title: How should retired ADR history remain reachable?
questions.question: How should retired ADR history remain reachable?
questions.answer:
ACC-5: Navigate from completed or historical capability links to the Wiki feature article first; the article links archived ADRs as sources. Keep the archive. S-024 already has an article; create one for S-022 while stating that its historical release packet is blocked, not completed.
WF-8F: Specs and Tasks are transient working artifacts, not product documentation. Once their useful content is turned into readable durable documentation and the exact change is verified on main, they are retired and discarded. The Wiki stores the reconciled retired Spec and later corrective Tasks update it; Blueprint, Wiki and Taskboard are the enduring and navigational surfaces.

questions.title: What establishes that an idea has become a shared design concept?
questions.question: What establishes that an idea has become a shared design concept?
questions.answer:
WF-2: An owner idea starts Align through grilling; owner and agent explicitly confirm a shared design concept, then blueprint it. Workflow: Idea -> Align through grilling -> confirmed design concept -> Blueprint -> recursive delivery loop.
FND-Q01: The workflow starts when the owner brings an idea and runs six phases: Idea -> Align (grilling to a shared design concept) -> Scope (Blueprint plus Specs, updating ADRs and docs) -> Plan (decompose into Tasks) -> Implement (loop over Tasks, tracked on TASKBOARD) -> Verify (to Spec and/or human QA). Destination is in BLUEPRINT, the Journey is a SPEC, each walked Path is a TASK. Prototype is optional, not a standard phase.
BPR-R1: The prior chat 'failed at the beginning' because it never actually started a grilling session. Had it started correctly, stopping the grilling session would have been the endpoint. The handoff should then carry the owner-authorized task and authority plus all needed context from the grilling notepad.

questions.title: How do confirmed answers reach durable owners?
questions.question: How do confirmed answers reach durable owners?
questions.answer:
FND-Q13: A grilling answer does not enter Canon inline. Settled material is promoted through ordinary scoped work: a TASK when the change is small and localized, or a SPEC with Tasks when it affects many things. Updating the Lexicon will usually be one Task, which performs and verifies the Canon update under the Contract.
TT-Q12: First clause: settled answers route by the whole ownership map (FND-Q21): definitions to the Lexicon, obligations to root controls, scoped capability choices to a Spec, cross-cutting choices to an ADR. Owner: locked answers go 'in some state of durable in the contract, docs, or specs' / 'in their durable places'.
PW-10: 'In their durable places in the workbench, wherever that may be.' The agent drew the landing map: Lexicon term and renames; Blueprint sentence; AGENTS and RUNBOOK rules; ADRs for the skills lane, note transport and claim-on-branch; manifest and templates; and a new Portable Workbench Spec owning the Tasks.
BPR-R3: This was a promotion and scoping handoff. The receiving chat should promote the grilling notepad into docs and Specs, using all the skills named for that process, so implementation could happen in a later step. It was not authorized to implement the promoted work in the same step.

questions.title: How does a grilling or handoff endpoint preserve the owner’s intended scope?
questions.question: How does a grilling or handoff endpoint preserve the owner’s intended scope?
questions.answer:
BPR-R1: The prior chat 'failed at the beginning' because it never actually started a grilling session. Had it started correctly, stopping the grilling session would have been the endpoint. The handoff should then carry the owner-authorized task and authority plus all needed context from the grilling notepad.
BPR-R3: This was a promotion and scoping handoff. The receiving chat should promote the grilling notepad into docs and Specs, using all the skills named for that process, so implementation could happen in a later step. It was not authorized to implement the promoted work in the same step.
V3-20: It authorizes the minimum complete single-repository v3 runway and preserves Kayden's owner-only promotion gate.
V3-20A: Promote the settled diary into the owning docs/spec, implement through red/green slices from refreshed integration, verify exact pushed heads, perform independent review, reconcile obsolete PR #42 after replacement proof, and open the final integration-to-main PR.
V3-20B: Merging to main, changing visibility or credentials, editing the private skills repository, importing Foundry machinery, broad guidebook or skill-catalog redesign, and claiming release without source/test/fresh-exercise proof.

questions.title: How does the product destination decompose into Specs and Tasks?
questions.question: How does the product destination decompose into Specs and Tasks?
questions.answer:
FND-Q01: The workflow starts when the owner brings an idea and runs six phases: Idea -> Align (grilling to a shared design concept) -> Scope (Blueprint plus Specs, updating ADRs and docs) -> Plan (decompose into Tasks) -> Implement (loop over Tasks, tracked on TASKBOARD) -> Verify (to Spec and/or human QA). Destination is in BLUEPRINT, the Journey is a SPEC, each walked Path is a TASK. Prototype is optional, not a standard phase.
FND-Q19: Blueprint owns the grand design, start to destination. A Spec is a journey step derived from Blueprint, active ADRs, evidence and Actuality: a smaller goalpost. Tasks are tracer-round vertical slices of a Spec, the smallest work fitting one useful context. The Workbench QAs the finished Spec branch before integration; integration is the owner's Human QA branch; he merges to main. A Task is one fresh context, one branch, a packet and a receipt.
WF-6: The Blueprint defines the product-level destination: count to 100. Each Spec is a mini-PRD, a scoped objective with its own destination, the next number to count to. Tasks do the counting. Stacked Specs together realize the Blueprint journey. TASKBOARD is the Kanban projection of progress and coordination, not truth or a second tracker.
WF-12: 'I want every spec completed before we call this done.' The rollout must complete the Blueprint rework and every Spec needed to establish the full workflow. The reworked Blueprint describes every rung and the full recursive Spec/Task loop (Create Spec -> Create Tasks -> Complete and Reconcile Tasks -> Verify Whole Spec -> Corrective Tasks -> Repeat Until Approved -> Integrate Spec). Future Blueprint capabilities outside that scope need no Specs now.

questions.title: What makes a Task a complete vertical execution slice?
questions.question: What makes a Task a complete vertical execution slice?
questions.answer:
TT-Q2: Task is a canonical concept, not an alias. TASK.md becomes its own artifact: a bounded, executable thin vertical slice of a Spec that carries blocking relationships so Tasks can complete in parallel, built with the tracer skill and picked up task after task with high-fidelity context. Task was meant to replace Ticket completely. The folder lifecycle applies to Tasks with no exception.
RB-Q2: Suggested A with sub-answer (ii): TASK.md is the single execution-slice artifact (context, branch and receipt unit); no level beneath Task; Ticket stays retired. Receipt is append-only, one row per run. "A is an aspiration, not a rule or a guarantee." New sizing rule: a Task expected to need more than one context unit should be a Spec that Tasks are cut from. He stated the unit as 250k tokens (revised to 200k in RB-Q2B).
FND-Q03: A Task is the smallest bounded work that fits one useful context; work expected to exceed one context unit (about 200k tokens, 'a goalpost, not a gate') is a Spec with Tasks. A context ends when its Task is complete and cleaned up: one Chat does one Task, then ends. The next context loads the Contract plus the Task (its Spec acceptance, optional handoff or notepad).

changes.to:
TT-Q2: Task is a canonical concept, not an alias. TASK.md becomes its own artifact: a bounded, executable thin vertical slice of a Spec that carries blocking relationships so Tasks can complete in parallel, built with the tracer skill and picked up task after task with high-fidelity context. Task was meant to replace Ticket completely. The folder lifecycle applies to Tasks with no exception.

FND-Q03: A Task is the smallest bounded work that fits one useful context; work expected to exceed one context unit (about 200k tokens, 'a goalpost, not a gate') is a Spec with Tasks. A context ends when its Task is complete and cleaned up: one Chat does one Task, then ends. The next context loads the Contract plus the Task (its Spec acceptance, optional handoff or notepad).

questions.title: How many Tasks should one Chat execute?
questions.question: How many Tasks should one Chat execute?
questions.answer:
TT-Q4: A Task should be 1:1 with a Chat. A few Chats for one Task is allowed but 'is not how it should be done': make the Task smaller, still vertical. One Chat should not do several Tasks: 'The chat should complete the task, clean up, and be done.' A dispatcher or director watches the Spec, writes handoffs and opens a new Chat per unblocked Task, and approves; it never executes Tasks itself.
TT-Q7: A fresh Chat is needed when the context is used up, and for the separate-context review. Handoffs are Markdown written for a new Chat. TT-Q4 adds that each Task gets its own Chat.
FND-Q03: A Task is the smallest bounded work that fits one useful context; work expected to exceed one context unit (about 200k tokens, 'a goalpost, not a gate') is a Spec with Tasks. A context ends when its Task is complete and cleaned up: one Chat does one Task, then ends. The next context loads the Contract plus the Task (its Spec acceptance, optional handoff or notepad).

questions.title: What must a Task receipt preserve after each run?
questions.question: What must a Task receipt preserve after each run?
questions.answer:
RB-Q1: Suggested A. Packet: TASK.md, the Spec acceptance lines the Task satisfies, the cited source and test paths, and the Contract; nothing else loads at entry. Receipt: commit SHA on the Task branch, tests run with result, docs touched, dirty files remaining, remaining gap; written into TASK.md and shown on the Taskboard. "Receipt" keeps its existing Lexicon meaning. Ticket-to-Task is the intended fix, not drift.
RB-Q2: Suggested A with sub-answer (ii): TASK.md is the single execution-slice artifact (context, branch and receipt unit); no level beneath Task; Ticket stays retired. Receipt is append-only, one row per run. "A is an aspiration, not a rule or a guarantee." New sizing rule: a Task expected to need more than one context unit should be a Spec that Tasks are cut from. He stated the unit as 250k tokens (revised to 200k in RB-Q2B).
RB-Q2A: Suggested A. The per-run receipt rows live in TASK.md as evidence; the Taskboard shows only a generated signal per active Task: run count and the latest run's branch, short SHA and dirty-file count. The full run table is never on the board.
RB-Q4: Suggested B: visibility plus a gate at the claim. Doctor gains attention-level git diagnostics (detached HEAD, untracked files in the controls, ADR and spec lanes) that never block; upstream distance joins the receipt row. close refuses a dirty tree or unpushed branch unless the receipt records that state and a reason. Doctor must not block on detached HEAD.

questions.title: When can a small change be a standalone Task?
questions.question: When can a small change be a standalone Task?
questions.answer:
E-9: At workbench/tasks/TK-XXXX/TASK.md beside the Specs, under the same ADR-000I folder lifecycle, in the same Workbench-unique TK- series. Its card has an empty spec field and moves through lanes on its own. Used for small localized changes; a standalone Task that outgrows one context unit becomes a Spec.
TT-Q3: A Workbench is a 'room' that holds many Workbenches and many Projects; each Project has exactly one Workbench of its own. A Workbench is one set of Contract and routing artifacts with one Blueprint. A Blueprint has many Specs and many Tasks; a Spec has many Tasks and many Chats; a Task maps to one Chat. Spec is the destination, Task the steps; small work may be a standalone Task.
FND-Q17c: Specs nest and block each other, the same way Tasks do: "SPECs can nest and block each other, same as tasks. we are changing that." In the same message he said a Task can be created and merged into integration without a Spec branch.
SCR-7A: The full hierarchy still runs: Dispatcher -> Worker -> Dispatcher -> Director, with Git integration -> Task branch -> integration -> integration. The Dispatcher sends the Worker from integration, verifies and merges the result, and the Director checks it on integration. No role works from main. A direct Task that outgrows one context or repeats one objective becomes a Spec.

questions.title: When does a corrective change need a new Spec?
questions.question: When does a corrective change need a new Spec?
questions.answer:
WF-8G: Route by scope and destination, not Task count. A gap against an existing Spec destination is fixed with reopened or corrective Tasks, even when several are needed. A new Spec is only for a distinct scoped objective with its own destination, such as investigating why the journey missed something. TASK.md holds active work state and TASKBOARD projects it; a Spec is open if it has Tasks on the board.
WF-8A: No reopen ceremony. A small corrective change against a retired Spec is a Task plus an update to the Wiki record of the reconciled retired Spec; SPEC.md is not resurrected, though a Spec branch may still carry the commit. 'What we wanted was the Spec, if that is right, then we are okay.'

questions.title: How should Task, Spec and integration branches relate?
questions.question: How should Task, Spec and integration branches relate?
questions.answer:
WF-7: Branches nest by delivery altitude: main contains integration; each Spec branch starts from integration; each Task branch starts from its Spec branch, preferably in its own worktree. Proven Task results merge into the Spec branch, and contained Task branches and worktrees are cleaned up after their results are preserved.
PW-6: Option 1: push the claim, read the remotes. claim creates the task branch from integration, commits the claim as its first commit and pushes at once; next and claim fetch all refs and overlay Task state from every remote tip. No direct claim commit on integration. The PR carries closure. A no-remote session falls back to local and says so.
FND-Q17c: Specs nest and block each other, the same way Tasks do: "SPECs can nest and block each other, same as tasks. we are changing that." In the same message he said a Task can be created and merged into integration without a Spec branch.
SCR-4B: Most Tasks are children of Specs and branch from the Spec work. A Task may instead be a direct child of the Blueprint when no intermediate Spec destination is needed; it branches from and merges straight into integration, which is metaphorically the Blueprint accumulation branch.

questions.question: How should branches and worktrees be cleaned up after delivery?

WF-7: Branches nest by delivery altitude: main contains integration; each Spec branch starts from integration; each Task branch starts from its Spec branch, preferably in its own worktree. PW-9: 'End clean up.' Recorded as the agent's interpretation: proof is a run that ends clean. Extend the round-trip test to start with nothing outside the clone, claim by pushing, and end with everything promoted, pushed and nothing left on the instance; demos are one real cloud session and a two-instance parallel run.

questions.title: What work should a dispatcher or director perform without executing Tasks?
questions.question: What work should a dispatcher or director perform without executing Tasks?
questions.answer: TT-Q4: A Task should be 1:1 with a Chat. A few Chats for one Task is allowed but 'is not how it should be done': make the Task smaller, still vertical. One Chat should not do several Tasks: 'The chat should complete the task, clean up, and be done.' A dispatcher or director watches the Spec, writes handoffs and opens a new Chat per unblocked Task, and approves; it never executes Tasks itself.

questions.title: How should the four agent stances be packaged and composed?
questions.question: How should the four agent stances be packaged and composed?
questions.answer:
WB-3: Package all four as portable stance skills. A stance says how an agent performs one task with the authority, responsibilities, good practices and composing skills suited to that work. Loading a stance never spawns a sub-agent; Builder, for example, must make sure review and verification happen. Keep cross-provider discovery: a stance stored under ~/.agents/skills/stances/ also needs a flat top-level symlink for Claude's one-level scan.
WB-12: A stance never grants, removes or transfers authority; it only changes how the model behaves within authority set before adoption. Every stance defines Purpose, Method / Posture, Obligations, and Completion / Exit Condition, and may add intrinsic constraints (e.g. Reviewer evaluates rather than quietly repairs). Changing stance creates no handoff, so one task may move Builder -> Reviewer -> Builder -> Reconciler uninterrupted.

questions.title: How far should an agent investigate before asking the owner or stopping?
questions.question: How far should an agent investigate before asking the owner or stopping?
questions.answer:
WB-6: The Workbench is autonomous within its standing authority. An arriving agent investigates the Contract, relevant ADRs, specs, task state, Wiki and project evidence, makes the best supported choice, and may construct the next decision from that evidence. Only when it cannot find a confident good next decision does it record the blocker and stop; the owner can open a grilling session on return. Platform safety and owner-only boundaries still apply.
WB-15: It does not create a next task for itself. An agent picks up its assigned task and works it autonomously; if information is missing it investigates and resolves it within that task from project evidence. Only when it cannot is a separate new task needed for a new agent, and the current agent does not manufacture that queue item or treat its absence as routine blockage.

questions.title: Which record authors work state, and what does the board project?
questions.question: Which record authors work state, and what does the board project?
questions.answer:
FND-Q02: TASKBOARD.md is the sole live project-management and Kanban view of the Frontier. It mostly renders active Specs and Tasks (priority, what is hot, progress, lanes, blockers) and holds no irreplaceable detail; Specs and Tasks own that. Agents update or regenerate it as Tasks move, and completed verified Specs and Tasks disappear so the board clears.
FND-Q02A: The underlying Specs and Tasks own substantive progress, issues, evidence and recoverable context; TASKBOARD.md renders and summarizes them and should hold as little irreplaceable context as possible. Sitrep must be able to read only the board for a complete active picture. Correction: do not call the board the navigation view. It is the Kanban and project-management view; it links to Tasks only because everything is navlinked. The Lexicon keeps the Context Map and Navlink hub role.
FND-Q21B: An altitude is a scope, not a file. Boundaries, Requirements, Acceptance and Evidence have owners at all three scopes; Destination (Blueprint, Spec) and Work state (Spec, Task) at two. Gaps are declared with a route. Boundaries splits inside one row: permission limits arrive by inherits, product exclusions by refines. Refined 2026-09-22 (Option B): the Taskboard is first-class as the project-wide representation of work state; TASKBOARD.json summarizes the Spec and Task records that author it.
FND-Q22A: Yes. The ownership map owns the maintained record of artifact classes, responsibilities, scopes, routes and relations, and answers where a truth belongs, including the Blueprint -> Spec -> Task relationships the other controls do not answer. It routes to the artifacts holding claims and never copies them or tracks live card instances. The Taskboard is a derived projection that summarizes Spec and Task records.

confirmation.basis: Each source answer was owner-settled in its grilling session, per the grilling ledger at 56b459da: FND-Q02, FND-Q02A, FND-Q21B, FND-Q22A (locked). questions.title: How should Spec and Task cards show hierarchy without double-counting work?
questions.question: How should Spec and Task cards show hierarchy without double-counting work?
questions.answer:
E-3: Both. A Task is a nested part of a Spec, so Spec and Task cards show progression, not duplicate work; a Spec card can count its child Tasks. A Spec cannot move to needsReview or complete until all its Tasks are in needsReview or complete. 'Not every Task has to belong to a Spec.' Specs always appear as cards.
FND-Q02A: The underlying Specs and Tasks own substantive progress, issues, evidence and recoverable context; TASKBOARD.md renders and summarizes them and should hold as little irreplaceable context as possible. Sitrep must be able to read only the board for a complete active picture. Correction: do not call the board the navigation view. It is the Kanban and project-management view; it links to Tasks only because everything is navlinked. The Lexicon keeps the Context Map and Navlink hub role.

questions.title: What does Needs review mean without imposing independent review on every Task?
questions.question: What does Needs review mean without imposing independent review on every Task?
questions.answer:
E-4C: Needs review is the independent reviewer (QA/verify) stage. Most Tasks go In progress -> Needs review -> Complete to await cleanup; work needing no independent review may go straight to Complete. Tasks collect in Needs review and Complete while their Spec is In progress, and move to Complete together when the Spec is reviewed.
E-3: Both. A Task is a nested part of a Spec, so Spec and Task cards show progression, not duplicate work; a Spec card can count its child Tasks. A Spec cannot move to needsReview or complete until all its Tasks are in needsReview or complete. 'Not every Task has to belong to a Spec.' Specs always appear as cards.
WF-8B: No per-Task independent-review ceremony just because it is a Task. Ordinary verification and proof are mandatory: red/green TDD, relevant tests green, exercising what was built, and preserved proof before handoff.
WF-8C: Keep a separate-context review whose unit is the assembled Spec and the combined result of its Tasks. A failed review is diagnostic, not blame: state what is wrong, create new corrective Tasks under the still-open Spec, update the Taskboard, execute and prove them, then present a fresh immutable Spec candidate. Passing lets the Spec branch move toward integration.

questions.title: How should Complete distinguish capture from final cleanup?
questions.question: How should Complete distinguish capture from final cleanup?
questions.answer:
E-11: Derived, never authored on the board: complete record in a live folder = ready to capture; in retired/ (ADR-000I) = captured, ready to delete; deleted = card drops. 'The state should show that we are good to move forward, not the taskboard. Updating that it's ready only to wipe it is pointless.' sitrep reports Complete as two counts.
E-1: Redirected answer: a generated TASKBOARD.json Agile Kanban board replaces TASKBOARD.md as the root contract artifact, with no TASKBOARD.md view. Six lanes (backlog, toDo, inProgress, blocked, needsReview, complete); cards keyed by WBID, no kind field; loose schema v1; owner = assignee; agents never write it. Complete cards 'stay until promoted to a durable place' and the record is deleted.
WF-8D: After a completed Task's results and needed proof are reconciled into the owning Spec, the Task is retired: its branch and worktree are deleted after verified containment, it leaves the hot Taskboard and ordinary pickup, and its TASK.md survives only as retired history reachable by an explicit historical route.

questions.title: What do Chat, Conversation and Thread mean?
questions.question: What do Chat, Conversation and Thread mean?
questions.answer:
TT-Q1: Chat. A Chat is the owner-visible working context in which a Conversation happens; many connected Chats form a Thread. Conversation is informal descriptive language, not a separate Workbench object. 'Codex Task' is rejected as the name. These are vocabulary, not structure.
TT-Q3: A Workbench is a 'room' that holds many Workbenches and many Projects; each Project has exactly one Workbench of its own. A Workbench is one set of Contract and routing artifacts with one Blueprint. A Blueprint has many Specs and many Tasks; a Spec has many Tasks and many Chats; a Task maps to one Chat. Spec is the destination, Task the steps; small work may be a standalone Task.

questions.title: How should Task replace Ticket while preserving historical identity?
questions.question: How should Task replace Ticket while preserving historical identity?
questions.answer:
WF-5: Task replaces Ticket as the execution-slice term across prose, tools, TASKBOARD columns, the to-tickets skill and new visible IDs. Existing TK-### identifiers inside completed Specs stay frozen as history and are never rewritten.
TT-Q2: Task is a canonical concept, not an alias. TASK.md becomes its own artifact: a bounded, executable thin vertical slice of a Spec that carries blocking relationships so Tasks can complete in parallel, built with the tracer skill and picked up task after task with high-fidelity context. Task was meant to replace Ticket completely. The folder lifecycle applies to Tasks with no exception.
TT-Q10: Task (Task replaces Ticket, WF-5). Newly allocated identifiers keep the TK-### form, with TK read as the Task prefix.

questions.title: What must a worker prove before handing off a Task result?
questions.question: What must a worker prove before handing off a Task result?
questions.answer:
WF-8: Tasks use red/green TDD, make relevant tests green, exercise what was built to confirm it works, and preserve proof before handoff. A separate context checks the assembled Spec. Integration is the assembled surface for owner Human QA, which can return work to Align before owner-only main promotion.
WF-8B: No per-Task independent-review ceremony just because it is a Task. Ordinary verification and proof are mandatory: red/green TDD, relevant tests green, exercising what was built, and preserved proof before handoff.
SCR-1: No separate-context QA or approval gate on a Task. A Task is a small one-time instruction: do the bounded step, update proof that Actuality moved closer to the destination, report back, end. The Worker self-checks that its claims are valid and backed by proof before hand-back; destination-level QA waits until the Spec is assembled.

questions.title: When is separate-context review required, and what unit does it inspect?
questions.question: When is separate-context review required, and what unit does it inspect?
questions.answer:
WB-4: Independent review is required only when work is ready to merge into integration: the proposed integration candidate gets a separate-context review before branches combine. That reviewer checks the candidate and its evidence, which is enough to challenge consequential claims, code changes and report recommendations. Earlier review, verification and audit are supports, not mandatory independent ceremonies.
WF-8B: No per-Task independent-review ceremony just because it is a Task. Ordinary verification and proof are mandatory: red/green TDD, relevant tests green, exercising what was built, and preserved proof before handoff.
WF-8C: Keep a separate-context review whose unit is the assembled Spec and the combined result of its Tasks. A failed review is diagnostic, not blame: state what is wrong, create new corrective Tasks under the still-open Spec, update the Taskboard, execute and prove them, then present a fresh immutable Spec candidate. Passing lets the Spec branch move toward integration.
SCR-2: When every Task in a Spec is complete. The unit is the assembled Spec and the combined Actuality and proof its Tasks produced; the check is whether the Spec's local destination was reached and moves the product toward the Blueprint destination. It has two agent checks: the Dispatcher's whole-Spec Verify/QA, then the Director's separate-context approval.
SCR-5: Nobody runs an approval gate per Task. The Worker self-verifies and hands back; the Dispatcher consumes the report, updates the view of Actuality and chooses the next step, for a Spec-scoped and a direct Blueprint Task alike. Merge or sequencing is coordination and containment, not destination-level QA.
SCR-7: Neither. Do not QA every Task and do not add a second reviewer for grouped brick-laying slices. Run toward the local destination the Spec describes, then do whole-Spec QA. A Task ends after its one attempt; if it missed, do not reopen it, create a new Task.
WF-8: Tasks use red/green TDD, make relevant tests green, exercise what was built to confirm it works, and preserve proof before handoff. A separate context checks the assembled Spec. Integration is the assembled surface for owner Human QA, which can return work to Align before owner-only main promotion.

changes.to:
WB-4: Independent review is required only when work is ready to merge into integration: the proposed integration candidate gets a separate-context review before branches combine. That reviewer checks the candidate and its evidence, which is enough to challenge consequential claims, code changes and report recommendations. Earlier review, verification and audit are supports, not mandatory independent ceremonies.
WF-8B: No per-Task independent-review ceremony just because it is a Task. Ordinary verification and proof are mandatory: red/green TDD, relevant tests green, exercising what was built, and preserved proof before handoff.
WF-8C: Keep a separate-context review whose unit is the assembled Spec and the combined result of its Tasks. A failed review is diagnostic, not blame: state what is wrong, create new corrective Tasks under the still-open Spec, update the Taskboard, execute and prove them, then present a fresh immutable Spec candidate. Passing lets the Spec branch move toward integration.
SCR-2: When every Task in a Spec is complete. The unit is the assembled Spec and the combined Actuality and proof its Tasks produced; the check is whether the Spec's local destination was reached and moves the product toward the Blueprint destination. It has two agent checks: the Dispatcher's whole-Spec Verify/QA, then the Director's separate-context approval.
SCR-5: Nobody runs an approval gate per Task. The Worker self-verifies and hands back; the Dispatcher consumes the report, updates the view of Actuality and chooses the next step, for a Spec-scoped and a direct Blueprint Task alike. Merge or sequencing is coordination and containment, not destination-level QA.
SCR-7: Neither. Do not QA every Task and do not add a second reviewer for grouped brick-laying slices. Run toward the local destination the Spec describes, then do whole-Spec QA. A Task ends after its one attempt; if it missed, do not reopen it, create a new Task.
WF-8: Tasks use red/green TDD, make relevant tests green, exercise what was built to confirm it works, and preserve proof before handoff. A separate context checks the assembled Spec. Integration is the assembled surface for owner Human QA, which can return work to Align before owner-only main promotion.

questions.title: What does owner Human QA evaluate, and where does it happen?
questions.question: What does owner Human QA evaluate, and where does it happen?
questions.answer:
FND-Q14: Two named gates. Spec QA gate: working branch into integration, triggered by the merge request; it checks every Task in the Spec is done and the branch is up to Spec, passing merges and failing denies. Human QA gate: integration into main; integration is the Human QA branch where the owner decides if work is ready or needs more. Human QA is not a release ceremony and is not batched by release.
WF-8: Tasks use red/green TDD, make relevant tests green, exercise what was built to confirm it works, and preserve proof before handoff. A separate context checks the assembled Spec. Integration is the assembled surface for owner Human QA, which can return work to Align before owner-only main promotion.
WF-9: Delivery repeats recursively. A failed Human QA result returns to Align and the design-concept/delivery loop at the appropriate scope.
SCR-6: Two acts by two parties. The Director approves each Spec its Dispatcher carries (a pass lets the Spec branch merge into integration and moves its card to Complete) and coordinates across Dispatchers. Owner Human QA comes after the Director has approved every Spec in the version or escalated blockers, and ends in the owner-only integration to main merge. What Human QA consists of is project-specific; here it is the owner monitoring, asking the Director questions and starting the next steps. Closure (features Wiki capture, record deletion) follows verification on main.

questions.answer:
WF-9: Delivery repeats recursively. A failed Human QA result returns to Align and the design-concept/delivery loop at the appropriate scope.
WF-8G: Route by scope and destination, not Task count. A gap against an existing Spec destination is fixed with reopened or corrective Tasks, even when several are needed. A new Spec is only for a distinct scoped objective with its own destination, such as investigating why the journey missed something. TASK.md holds active work state and TASKBOARD projects it; a Spec is open if it has Tasks on the board.
WF-12: 'I want every spec completed before we call this done.' The rollout must complete the Blueprint rework and every Spec needed to establish the full workflow. The reworked Blueprint describes every rung and the full recursive Spec/Task loop (Create Spec -> Create Tasks -> Complete and Reconcile Tasks -> Verify Whole Spec -> Corrective Tasks -> Repeat Until Approved -> Integrate Spec). Future Blueprint capabilities outside that scope need no Specs now.

questions.title: What does a release-readiness review establish and authorize?
questions.question: What does a release-readiness review establish and authorize?
questions.answer:
BPR-8F1: Asking whether a candidate is ready for main authorizes an independent release review and a verdict only, not merge or publication. Kayden keeps approval and merge authority for integration to main. An agent may create the release PR only when explicitly asked, and Kayden still approves and merges it.
BPR-8E: When Kayden asks whether a candidate is ready for main, the independent reviewer checks the Blueprint boundary: destination narrative and whole-product constraints only; no version chronology, live status, Spec inventory, evidence or displaced ADR/Spec/Runbook content; ADR links selective, active and coherent; each new ADR has a recorded Blueprint relevance disposition. Mechanical checks support structure and links but cannot replace semantic review.
WF-8: Tasks use red/green TDD, make relevant tests green, exercise what was built to confirm it works, and preserve proof before handoff. A separate context checks the assembled Spec. Integration is the assembled surface for owner Human QA, which can return work to Align before owner-only main promotion.
WF-8B: No per-Task independent-review ceremony just because it is a Task. Ordinary verification and proof are mandatory: red/green TDD, relevant tests green, exercising what was built, and preserved proof before handoff.

confirmation.basis: Each source answer was owner-settled in its grilling session, per the grilling ledger at 56b459da: BPR-8F1, BPR-8E, WF-8, WF-8B (locked). questions.question: What should remain after a Spec becomes delivered product knowledge?
questions.answer:
WF-8F: Specs and Tasks are transient working artifacts, not product documentation. Once their useful content is turned into readable durable documentation and the exact change is verified on main, they are retired and discarded. questions.title: How should later corrections maintain knowledge from a retired Spec?
questions.question: How should later corrections maintain knowledge from a retired Spec?
questions.answer:
WF-8A: No reopen ceremony. A small corrective change against a retired Spec is a Task plus an update to the Wiki record of the reconciled retired Spec; SPEC.md is not resurrected, though a Spec branch may still carry the commit. 'What we wanted was the Spec, if that is right, then we are okay.'
WF-8G: Route by scope and destination, not Task count. A gap against an existing Spec destination is fixed with reopened or corrective Tasks, even when several are needed. A new Spec is only for a distinct scoped objective with its own destination, such as investigating why the journey missed something. questions.title: What does an objective notepad preserve, and whom does it belong to?
questions.question: What does an objective notepad preserve, and whom does it belong to?
questions.answer:
TT-Q9: A handoff is Markdown for a new Chat or agent; a notepad is the JSON working record; a notepad belongs to its objective, not to the Chat, model or host that created it (ADR-000L).
PW-5: Promote-before-end is the goal for almost every session: promote settled claims, append the receipt, push, let the notepad die. With an amendment: 'we can have the notepads and handoffs stay if needed... we should be able to commit them for a bit if we need to, undoing the lock on them never being committed.' Committed notes are transport, not evidence; privacy rules stand; ADR-0051 stays optional.

questions.title: What makes a handoff useful to its receiving context?
questions.question: What makes a handoff useful to its receiving context?
questions.answer:
BPR-R2: A human-readable Markdown handoff. The handoff skill 'already should require' this, and its wording should say explicitly that a handoff is a human-readable Markdown file. The JSON notepad stays the working context and is not the handoff.
BPR-R4: The handoff succeeds when the new chat can complete the task it was created for, using the authority and context the handoff carries. Success is not measured by completing ceremony after the handoff file exists.
BPR-R1: The prior chat 'failed at the beginning' because it never actually started a grilling session. Had it started correctly, stopping the grilling session would have been the endpoint. The handoff should then carry the owner-authorized task and authority plus all needed context from the grilling notepad.
TT-Q7: A fresh Chat is needed when the context is used up, and for the separate-context review. Handoffs are Markdown written for a new Chat. TT-Q4 adds that each Task gets its own Chat.
TT-Q9: A handoff is Markdown for a new Chat or agent; a notepad is the JSON working record; a notepad belongs to its objective, not to the Chat, model or host that created it (ADR-000L).

questions.question: What is the reference Template meant to provide?
questions.answer:

questions.title: What real Template upgrade must each Workbench version prove?
questions.question: What real Template upgrade must each Workbench version prove?
questions.answer:
BPR-7A: Every Workbench version must be proved by successfully updating Example_Workbench (now Workbench Template) to that version. Genesis for a project with no Blueprint should seed a starting Blueprint and a prepared grilling notepad grounded in the project's evidence, and an update should not silently treat an existing Blueprint as owner-validated. Those mechanisms are future capabilities and must not be claimed before built and verified.
FND-Q12: The Workbench_Template is the answer: each release must 'fully build a working template ... that a room can turn into its own project', and updating the Template to the new version is the release gate.
BPR-7B1: For v3.2 it is enough that LLM Workbench applies the newly settled ownership and routing rules to update Workbench Template successfully. Fresh-copy personalization, prepared project grilling, Genesis completion and validation of a personalized Workbench are future capabilities; v3.2 must not claim them.

questions.title: What complete cycle on another room establishes workflow mission success?
questions.question: What complete cycle on another room establishes workflow mission success?
questions.answer:
WF-11: Mission success is one full cycle on another workbench: LLM_Workbench creates or updates it, a grilling session runs, the contract and Specs are created or updated, Tasks are created and executed correctly, and the Spec is verified and on integration for owner review. 'Once that cycle is complete on another workbench we will say mission success.'
WF-12: 'I want every spec completed before we call this done.' The rollout must complete the Blueprint rework and every Spec needed to establish the full workflow. The reworked Blueprint describes every rung and the full recursive Spec/Task loop (Create Spec -> Create Tasks -> Complete and Reconcile Tasks -> Verify Whole Spec -> Corrective Tasks -> Repeat Until Approved -> Integrate Spec). Future Blueprint capabilities outside that scope need no Specs now.

questions.title: What proves a cloud or parallel-instance run is portable end to end?
questions.question: What proves a cloud or parallel-instance run is portable end to end?
questions.answer:
PW-9: 'End clean up.' Recorded as the agent's interpretation: proof is a run that ends clean. Extend the round-trip test to start with nothing outside the clone, claim by pushing, and end with everything promoted, pushed and nothing left on the instance; demos are one real cloud session and a two-instance parallel run.
PW-1: Portable Workbench = 'a fully packaged and deployable agentic harness': everything an agent needs is in the Git repository, so any agent, or several at once in the cloud, can clone it, do authorized work, push, and clean up after itself. All three renames accepted: support-root layout, host portability, ownership origin model. The success criterion gains 'cleaning up after itself'.
PW-6: Option 1: push the claim, read the remotes. claim creates the task branch from integration, commits the claim as its first commit and pushes at once; next and claim fetch all refs and overlay Task state from every remote tip. No direct claim commit on integration. The PR carries closure. A no-remote session falls back to local and says so.

questions.title: Which older release and continuity commitments remain live obligations?
questions.question: Which older release and continuity commitments remain live obligations?
questions.answer:
FND-Q16: Specs, Tasks, DQCs, notepads and handoffs are transient scaffolding. Once their useful content reaches durable owners and the intended result exists, the implementation and its maintained documentation become the continuing reference and the scaffolding is no longer needed. Obsolete release promises become historical or superseded; still-needed obligations remain reachable until resolved. Correct or expand existing ADRs rather than add slightly different decisions; a new ADR must add a valuable architectural lens or layer and explain why the decision was made.
V3-18: Implement directly in the public LLM Workbench repository from current integration; do not wait on or route through unfinished Forge producer work.
V3-18A: Directly on an isolated codex/ branch from refreshed origin/integration in LLM Workbench.
V3-18B: One. Skills, templates, guidebook edits, focused tools, migrations, and proof ship in LLM Workbench; there is no [the owner's private skills repository] PR.
V3-20: It authorizes the minimum complete single-repository v3 runway and preserves Kayden's owner-only promotion gate.
V3-20A: Promote the settled diary into the owning docs/spec, implement through red/green slices from refreshed integration, verify exact pushed heads, perform independent review, reconcile obsolete PR #42 after replacement proof, and open the final integration-to-main PR.
V3-20B: Merging to main, changing visibility or credentials, editing the private skills repository, importing Foundry machinery, broad guidebook or skill-catalog redesign, and claiming release without source/test/fresh-exercise proof.
V3-24A: The workbench/ layout and manifest; the 12-skill missing-only brand-new-install contract; updates to existing setup/upgrade instructions and affected paths; focused deterministic checks; one fresh Genesis proof; and one existing-project Adoption proof.
U313-1: Yes - all six land in v3.1.3, TK-005 first.
U313-1A: All six: TK-001, TK-002, TK-003, TK-005, TK-006, TK-007. Order starts at TK-005.
U313-1B: This session owns all six.
E-6: Two new v4 build Specs added to S-00O's build list, not folded into S-00P. Final order ('Yes, lets do it'): (1) WBID Spec (uppercase width 4 allocator, dual-form lookup, ADR-0041 amendment); (2) board Spec (TASKBOARD.json, lanes, lane function, sitrep; ADR-000E and ADR-0013 amendments); (3) S-00P TK-002..TK-005 rewriting controls once around the new board; (4) S-00O release.
WB-11: Build only the four stance skills, the reduced ordinary entry route (AGENTS.md -> RUNBOOK.md -> LEXICON.md), and the feedback-report workflow and format in the existing feedback lane before running the first report. Implement it step by step.

changes.to:
FND-Q16: Specs, Tasks, DQCs, notepads and handoffs are transient scaffolding. Once their useful content reaches durable owners and the intended result exists, the implementation and its maintained documentation become the continuing reference and the scaffolding is no longer needed. Obsolete release promises become historical or superseded; still-needed obligations remain reachable until resolved. Correct or expand existing ADRs rather than add slightly different decisions; a new ADR must add a valuable architectural lens or layer and explain why the decision was made.
V3-18: Implement directly in the public LLM Workbench repository from current integration; do not wait on or route through unfinished Forge producer work.
V3-18A: Directly on an isolated codex/ branch from refreshed origin/integration in LLM Workbench.
V3-18B: One. Skills, templates, guidebook edits, focused tools, migrations, and proof ship in LLM Workbench; there is no [the owner's private skills repository] PR.

V3-20B: Merging to main, changing visibility or credentials, editing the private skills repository, importing Foundry machinery, broad guidebook or skill-catalog redesign, and claiming release without source/test/fresh-exercise proof.
V3-24A: The workbench/ layout and manifest; the 12-skill missing-only brand-new-install contract; updates to existing setup/upgrade instructions and affected paths; focused deterministic checks; one fresh Genesis proof; and one existing-project Adoption proof.

questions.title: What should a setup-only Round One establish?
questions.question: What should a setup-only Round One establish?
questions.answer:
WB-1: Build the redesigned workflow, then complete Round One: a fresh agent uses the reduced route, Wiki and ADRs to confirm the Workbench is set up correctly. Only after Round One succeeds, produce a reviewed, evidence-backed harness-feedback report and show cold continuation to its accepted next action. The report must not authorize or include a repair to the harness it evaluates.
WB-11: Build only the four stance skills, the reduced ordinary entry route (AGENTS.md -> RUNBOOK.md -> LEXICON.md), and the feedback-report workflow and format in the existing feedback lane before running the first report. Implement it step by step.
WB-13: Round One is not a harness-feedback or review test. It succeeds when a fresh agent uses the reduced entry route, consults the Wiki and relevant ADRs, and determines the Workbench is set up correctly. Passing that orientation-and-configuration proof is mission success for Round One; review and feedback testing follow afterward.
WB-14: The agent inspects the Workbench using the intended route and returns to the current chat to confirm it works. Round One creates no feedback report, handoff, checkpoint, self-created task or other prose artifact.

questions.title: What is a landmark, and how long does it live?
questions.question: What is a landmark, and how long does it live?
questions.answer:
LD-2: Codex definition (proposal-001) locked; landmark holds exploration before the canonical map; accepted direction reflected in the Blueprint.
LD-3: A landmark is an evolving feature/framework account, not a Spec or PRD. It has its own structured record alongside the readable Wiki explanation.
LD-7: No universal parent Spec. A landmark is not a Spec or PRD and is not implemented itself. Bounded Specs and Tasks deliver work; several Specs may contribute to one landmark explanation. Links expose those contributions.
LD-18: A landmark is an evolving account of a Workbench feature or framework. It is never implemented itself: Specs and Tasks implement, and the landmark tracks them as they evolve. It must earn a place in the contract (for LLM_Workbench mostly its Blueprint). It has a Wiki page and durable place from the start, may never leave the board, and retires only when nothing lives solely on it. ADRs are routing and decision records, not the delivery path.

questions.title: What do the eight documentation steps measure?
questions.question: What do the eight documentation steps measure?
questions.answer:
LD-12: Cards represent destination concepts, distinct from constituent grilling prompts. Mixed progress shown as percentage distributions for questions and landmarks; no single card lane/reset lifecycle. Exact steps Idea, Aligning, Confirmed, Mapped, Planned, Journey, Review, Verified remain locked. Tracker generated; folder placement behavior needs reconciliation with corrected model.
LD-23: Destination concept/documentation progress toward durable destination, displayed as per-step percentage distribution. Each related item contributes actual step or mixed fractions totaling one. Same calculation for landmarks/Workbench, with shared items counted once. Tracker additive/documentation; Taskboard implementation. No child-completion proxy or reset lifecycle.

questions.title: What makes a concept Confirmed after Align, and how do the later steps advance?
questions.question: What makes a concept Confirmed after Align, and how do the later steps advance?
questions.answer: GX-1: Aligned is a locked grilling answer with no Tracker card yet. At session completion each locked answer is added to an existing DQC, or to a new DQC where it evolves independently, which makes it Confirmed. Mapped uses selective ADRs from DQCs where warranted, then Specs as small destinations. Planned means ready Tasks. Journey means implementation. Review is distinct code and QA review with TDD proof. Verified compares delivered work against the DQC's expected understanding and result. Existing workflow skills maintain DQCs at each step, preferably through one focused DQC primitive; there is no DQC-specific review skill.

questions.title: What happens to a Task whose one attempt missed?
questions.question: What happens to a Task whose one attempt missed?
questions.answer: SCR-8: A Task that did not complete its run is not discarded: its TASK.md is the record until the Spec is cleaned up into the features Wiki. Its hand-back report stays as diagnostic proof in the Spec evidence. Its card returns to In progress and a new Task, named for its objective (the card title, not the WBID), fixes what the check found, starting fresh unless the Dispatcher deliberately builds on the old tip. The worktree is removed at hand-back; the missed branch is named in the Spec evidence and its deletion is covered by the Director's Spec approval. A Worker that stops unexpectedly leaves what it documented as it went; updating the card is part of finishing a Task.
